tiers.1: scholarly work by economists, in any venue: journal articles, working papers, books, chapters, commission reports, and their essays or articles in magazines. "Economist" means an economics appointment, degree, address or affiliation shown in or near the text, or an established record as an economist. Anything in a core economics venue (top five, JEP, JEL, AER P&P, NBER working papers and the NBER Economics of AI volume) is tier 1 regardless of author. Kansantaloudellinen aikakauskirja is a core venue for the Finnish strand (2026-10-12).
tiers.2: texts by non-economists, whatever the venue, and short-form commentary even by economists (blog comments, forum replies, magazine or online debates, unless a turn is itself a substantive scholarly argument).
tiers.decision: Maintainer decision of 2026-10-11 (README D2), shared with the economics-growth pack. It replaces the rule of 2026-10-09, under which magazines were tier 2 whatever the author. Each source and lead carries a one-line tierBasis. Calls of 2026-10-12: economist testimony in the 1955 hearings (Buckingham, Nourse) tier 1; the 1966 Commission main report tier 2 and its economist-written appendices tier 1; ETLA Brief 22 tier 1; the Triple Revolution memorandum tier 2; KAK texts tier 1 (a core venue for the Finnish strand); the Hanson–Yudkowsky 2008 blog debate tier 2 (not in this pack). Earliest located is computed within tier 1; the tier-2 earliest is shown separately (role earliest-located-tier-2).

propositions.statement: A text analyses computers, automation or AI as ordinary technical change, without a separate category for machine cognition.
propositions.criterion: A tier-1 text dated before 2015 that discusses computers, automation or AI and analyses them with the tools used for technical change in general (factor-augmenting or skill-biased change, capital deepening), with no separate category for machine cognition.
propositions.note: Text-level. Whether this describes the field before 2015 is assessed under M09 from the set of such texts. Contesting evidence: a pre-2015 tier-1 text that treats machine intelligence as distinct in kind. The 2015 cutoff is a working boundary set by the brief.

propositions.statement: AI's economic effect is the automation of tasks previously performed by labour.
propositions.criterion: A text that models or describes AI's economic effect as machines taking over tasks previously done by labour, within a task framework (tasks allocated between capital and labour).

propositions.statement: AI is a general-purpose technology whose measured productivity effects lag its adoption.
propositions.criterion: A text that calls AI a general-purpose technology and states that measured productivity gains lag adoption because of complementary investment (for example a J-curve or a productivity paradox).
propositions.note: Deliberately a conjunction: a text that calls AI a general-purpose technology without the lag bears on it (missing: the lag); a text that states a lag without the general-purpose framing likewise.

propositions.statement: AI's economic function is to lower the cost of prediction.
propositions.criterion: A text that defines or treats AI's economic function as prediction and draws consequences from a fall in its cost (for example for the value of complements such as judgement or data).

propositions.statement: Machines could come to perform every task, including newly created tasks, at lower cost than human labour.
propositions.criterion: A text that states or models the possibility that machines perform all or nearly all tasks, including tasks created later, at lower cost than human labour. Texts that assume new tasks in which labour is cheaper keep appearing bear on it without meeting it.
propositions.note: Bears on whether mainstream economics 'largely ignores' the possibility of AI surpassing human capability in all tasks. An omission claim needs searched-scope evidence, not a single silence.

propositions.statement: AI or automation can lower the labour share, wages or employment of some groups.
propositions.criterion: A text that states or models that AI or automation lowers the labour share, wages or employment for some or all workers.

propositions.statement: The distributional effects of AI call for redistribution, taxation or other compensating policy.
propositions.criterion: A text that argues for redistribution, taxation or another compensating policy in response to distributional effects of AI or automation.

propositions.statement: Occupations' exposure to computerisation or AI can be measured from their task content.
propositions.criterion: A text that estimates the share of jobs, occupations or tasks exposed or susceptible to computerisation or AI from task or occupation descriptions.

propositions.statement: AI's aggregate productivity effect over about the next decade, as estimated at the time of writing.
propositions.criterion: A text that gives a stated estimate of AI's effect on aggregate productivity or GDP over a horizon of about ten years from the text's date. The figure and horizon are recorded; the proposition is neutral as to size.
propositions.note: Recorded as a quantity, not a judgement of modest or large. A material quantitative claim under the editorial policy, so every figure needs a targeted recheck.

propositions.statement: Mainstream economics engaged with machine intelligence as a research topic only recently.
propositions.criterion: Not a criterion for a single passage. Assessed from the dated record: the earliest located tier-1 texts, within the searched scope, whose subject is AI, automation by AI or machine intelligence; plus explicit self-descriptions in tier-1 texts of the field as new or neglected. Tier-2 and outside texts are context.
propositions.note: The maintainer's prior, to be tested, not confirmed. Self-descriptions ('economists have only recently…') are evidence of how authors saw the field, not proof of absence of earlier work.
